conceptTag: MoviePass lost money on every ticket
readerTitle: MoviePass: the more it grew, the more it lost
caseNote: 실제 기업 (MoviePass, Helios and Matheson, AMC Stubs A-List) + 가상 계산 (회원 한 명의 한 달) + 가상 적용 (B2B IT 지원 회사)
insight: 정액제에서 고객 한 명이 남기는 돈은 가격이 아니라 사용량이 정한다. 남들보다 지나치게 싼 가격은 가장 많이 쓰는 고객부터 끌어모은다.
misconception: 건당 손해가 나도 회원이 충분히 많아지면 규모가 손실을 메워 준다.

sources.text: Helios and Matheson Analytics, SEC 공시 (2017년 8월 MoviePass 지분 인수 및 $9.95 요금 발표, 2018년 현금 부족·긴급 차입 관련 8-K/10-Q)
주요 언론 보도 (CNBC, Variety, The New York Times 등): 회원 수 100만 명(2017년 12월), 300만 명 이상(2018년 중반), 2018년 7월 서비스 중단과 $500만 긴급 차입
AMC Entertainment 보도자료 (2018년 6월): AMC Stubs A-List 출시, 월 $19.95, 주 3편
MoviePass 서비스 종료 공지 (2019년 9월), Helios and Matheson 파산 신청 (2020년 1월)
National Association of Theatre Owners: 2017년 미국 평균 영화 티켓 가격 (약 $8.97)

factChecks.note: 요금 인하 전 회원 수 "약 2만 명"은 언론 보도 기준입니다. 2017년 12월 100만 명 돌파, 2018년 중반 300만 명 이상도 보도로 확인하세요.
2018년 7월 결제 실패로 서비스가 중단되었고 모회사가 $500만을 긴급 차입했습니다. 당시 공시에 월 현금 적자가 약 $2,170만이라는 수치가 있었다고 알려져 있으나, 카드에는 "tens of millions of dollars a month"로만 적었습니다. 공시 원문을 확인하세요.
AMC Stubs A-List 출시 가격 $19.95와 주 3편 조건은 2018년 6월 보도자료 기준입니다. 이후 주별로 가격이 달라졌습니다.
주요 극장 체인(AMC 등)이 MoviePass와의 수익 공유를 거부했다는 내용은 언론 보도로 확인하세요. 2021년 FTC 합의, 2022년 경영진 기소는 이 레슨의 범위 밖이라 넣지 않았습니다.
9번 카드 IT 지원 사례는 가상입니다: 40명 × $30 = 월 $1,200, 기술자 비용 시간당 $60이면 월 20시간에서 본전입니다.

cards.title: MoviePass: the more it grew, the more it lost
body: In 2017, MoviePass offered a deal that sounded too good: one movie in a theater every day for $9.95 a month.
Millions of people signed up. And every time one of them watched a film, MoviePass paid the theater full price for the ticket.

image.label: A crowd rushing into a cinema while a wallet drains
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 영화관 입구로 사람들이 줄지어 들어가고, 옆에 놓인 큰 지갑에서 동전이 한 명 들어갈 때마다 하나씩 빠져나감. 실제 MoviePass, AMC 로고나 카드 디자인은 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: You just bought a movie subscription company.
body: It's 2017. Your service has a small base of members paying a high monthly fee. Each time a member sees a film, you pay the theater the full ticket price.
Investors want growth. What price do you set?

options.text: $9.95 for a movie a day. Win millions of members, then use that size to get theater deals
options.feedback: You get growth fast. But every visit is cash out the door until theaters agree to a deal, and the cheapest plan pulls in the heaviest moviegoers first.

options.text: A price that covers the visits a typical member makes, with a monthly cap
options.feedback: Growth is slower, but each member leaves money from day one. You negotiate with theaters from a business that can survive a no.

options.text: Keep the high price and the small, loyal base
options.feedback: Each member stays profitable, which is safe. But you may never reach the size that makes theaters want to talk.

cards.title: MoviePass chose $9.95.
body: In August 2017, data firm Helios and Matheson bought a majority stake in MoviePass and cut the price to $9.95 a month for a movie a day.
Members jumped from roughly 20,000 to over a million by the end of the year, and to more than 3 million in 2018.
But MoviePass didn't own any theaters. Members paid at the box office with a MoviePass card, and MoviePass covered the full ticket.

cards.title: One member's month.
body: Using a rounded US average ticket of about $9. In big cities, one ticket often cost more than the whole monthly fee.

cards.title: In a flat-fee plan, usage sets the margin.
body: **Unit economics** asks what one customer leaves you after the costs that come with serving them. With a flat fee, that number isn't fixed. It shrinks with every use.

MoviePass bet that light users would pay for heavy ones. But a price that's only a bargain for frequent moviegoers attracts frequent moviegoers. The customers who joined fastest were the ones who cost the most.

image.label: A seesaw tipping toward heavy users
image.brief: 시소 인포그래픽. 한쪽에 "Light users" 사람 몇 명(가볍게), 다른 쪽에 팝콘을 든 "Heavy users" 사람이 많이 앉아 시소가 크게 기울어짐. 가운데 받침에 "$9.95" 라벨.

cards.title: More members meant bigger losses.
body: When each member loses money, growth doesn't fix it. It multiplies it. MoviePass was reportedly burning tens of millions of dollars a month by 2018.
In July 2018 the service went down after it couldn't pay for tickets, and its parent took a $5 million emergency loan. It then tried caps, blocked popular films and changed rules often. Members left.
MoviePass shut down in September 2019. Its parent filed for bankruptcy in January 2020.

cards.title: The theater owner made it work.
body: In June 2018, AMC launched Stubs A-List: $19.95 a month for up to three movies a week.
The difference was ownership. A seat in a show that runs anyway costs AMC almost nothing, and members buy popcorn and drinks at a high margin. MoviePass paid full price for that same seat.

The lesson isn't "subscriptions fail." It's that a member's value depends on what each use actually costs you. A retailer's free-delivery club works on the same logic: only when it controls delivery costs.

image.label: Two cinema seats with different price tags
image.brief: 영화관 좌석 두 개를 나란히. 왼쪽 좌석 태그 "Paid to the theater: full ticket", 오른쪽 좌석 태그 "Owner's empty seat: almost $0" + 팝콘 아이콘. 실제 극장 브랜드 표시 없음.

cards.title: Losing money early isn't always wrong.
body: Many businesses lose money on early customers on purpose. That can work when there's a believable path to each customer turning positive: costs that fall with scale, prices that can rise, or revenue from somewhere else.
MoviePass hoped for data, ads and a share of theater sales. Major chains largely refused to share. Ask what must be true for one customer to make money, and check whether it's in your control.
cards.softwareNote: Unlimited plans for AI tools face the same trap. Each request has a real computing cost, so the heaviest users can cost far more than they pay. Many products now cap usage or charge by volume.

cards.title: Now it's an IT support firm.
body: You provide IT help to small offices. A prospect with 40 staff wants unlimited support for $30 a person per month. That's $1,200 a month.
Your technicians cost about $60 an hour. The client mentions their last provider dropped them for calling too often.

options.text: Accept. A big client helps growth, and lighter clients will balance it out
options.feedback: You gain a big account, but past 20 hours a month you lose money. And they've told you they're a heavy user.

options.text: Offer a plan with set hours included, and bill extra hours
options.feedback: You may lose the deal, but if they sign, every hour is covered. Heavy use becomes revenue instead of a loss.
You avoid the risk, but also a client who could be profitable on better terms.

cards.title: If one customer loses money, more customers lose more.
body: Before pricing a flat-fee plan, work out what your heaviest customer costs. They're the first to sign up.
**Try it today:** pick your best deal or plan. Write down what it costs you when your most active customer uses it fully.
